_purpose: PCI DSS 6.4.3(c) requires a written inventory of every script on the payment page, each with a justification. The prose inventory lives beside the prod CSP it describes, at OBRS-backend/deploy/prod/PAYMENT-PAGE-SCRIPT-INVENTORY.md. THIS file is the machine-readable half of it for the surfaces only this repo can change, and scripts/check-payment-page-scripts.mjs enforces it. Edit both together.
_note: The two repos each gate what they can break: this file vs the frontend's scripts and netlify.toml, and CspAllowlistMatchesInventoryTest vs the prod Caddyfile. Neither can read the other's tree, so the prose document is the seam - keep the origin lists in the two files in step by hand when the policy changes.
_origins_note: OBRS-882: `origins` is an ARRAY because one file can load from more than one vendor, and the single-string `origin` it replaced could not say so - a loader's SECOND vendor satisfied the old rule 4 while appearing in no inventory and no CSP. check-payment-page-scripts.mjs now compares this list against the https origins the file actually names, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS.

scriptLoaders.why: Required to take card payments at all. omise.js defines both window.Omise and window.OmiseCard; OmiseCard renders the card fields inside an iframe on cdn.omise.co and posts a token back, which is what keeps the PAN off this origin (OBRS-391). Removing it would mean collecting the PAN ourselves.

Google Identity Services - the 'Sign in with Google' button. Loaded from TypeScript rather than index.html specifically so it stays OFF the payment page (OBRS-719 AC 3). The hl locale must be a query param on the script URL; GIS exposes no initialize() option for it (OBRS-90).
Google Maps JS for the home-page route map. NOT a payment-page script - listed because maps.googleapis.com is in the site-wide script-src and a single CSP header cannot be route-scoped.

GA4 (gtag.js) and Microsoft Clarity, added by OBRS-867 to answer where customers drop out of the booking funnel - OBRS-862 and OBRS-872 are both blocked on that. STATE IT PLAINLY: AnalyticsService.init() runs in the app shell and AnalyticsTagsService.load() fires on the consent stream, so once a customer accepts, BOTH tags are on EVERY route INCLUDING /payment. These are payment-page scripts. What makes that acceptable is the same argument as for the rest of this page: card fields live in an iframe on cdn.omise.co, so same-origin policy denies these scripts - and anything injected into them - any access to the PAN (OBRS-391). Two further limits are load-bearing rather than incidental: nothing is injected until AnalyticsConsentService reports 'granted' (a PDPA requirement that doubles as a smaller attack surface), and an empty ID is a total no-op, so CI and every fresh clone run with no third-party script at all. What this does NOT buy is integrity of the bytes those two origins serve - see section 3 of the prose inventory; the residual is accepted on the same terms as Omise's and Google's.

_obrs1135_note: jquery.min.js was removed from this list, from BOTH scripts[] arrays in angular.json, and from package.json (OBRS-1135). It had zero call sites: one grep hit in src/ and it is a comment, no `$(`, no `import from 'jquery'`, and npm ls showed nothing depended on it. The prose inventory justified it as 'Bootstrap 5's JS still expects it in this app's setup' - that was measurably false. bootstrap.min.js does name jQuery 16 times, but only through getjQuery(), which returns null when window.jQuery is absent and skips registering the jQuery plugin bridge; bootstrap@5.3.3 peerDependencies lists @popperjs/core alone. Measured: initial bundle 1,851,483 -> 1,771,928 B. NOTE FOR WHOEVER EDITS scripts[] NEXT: this used to warn that check-payment-page-scripts.mjs read architect.build.options ONLY, leaving the architect.test.options copy ungated and kept in step by hand. It is gated now - rule 6 of that file compares the two arrays to each other, load order included (OBRS-1150), driven by self-test cases covering both directions of the OBRS-1135 near-miss. Rewritten rather than deleted: a note still describing a hand-kept discipline would send the next reader looking for one that no longer exists.
_obrs1311_note: https://hkupaujkdvdrqmtifgsm.supabase.co is SIT's Supabase Storage project, in img-src, holding the screenshots customers attach to usability reports. Four surfaces bind the backend's absolute public URL straight into : the admin report detail modal and its lightbox, the customer My-reports modal, the shared follow-up timeline, and the edit form's preview of already-uploaded images. img-src and not connect-src because nothing fetches these over XHR; a named host and not https://*.supabase.co because that would trust every Supabase project on the internet. THE REF DIFFERS FROM PROD'S ON PURPOSE — SIT and prod are separate Supabase projects, so this is the one origin where the two policies must NOT carry the same string; prod's is suacqfatxqedgntpsrfr and lives in the Caddyfile. What the value rests on, heaviest first: it was MEASURED to exist — GET https://.supabase.co/storage/v1/bucket answers 400, i.e. storage-api replying, while an invented ref does not resolve at all — and it was read off application-sit.yml's pooler username (postgres.hkupaujkdvdrqmtifgsm), the same route OBRS-206 took for prod before confirming it on the VM. ONLY THE REF TRAVELS THAT WAY, NEVER THE WHOLE HOST: application-prod.yml says in its own comment (OBRS-401/429) that the pooler HOSTNAME was copied verbatim from the dashboard and must not be derived, because Supabase assigns the region prefix per project. Storage is .supabase.co with no region in it, which is why the ref alone suffices here and is not a licence to guess the database host. check-payment-page-scripts.mjs rejects prod's ref by name, because that mistake is invisible under Report-Only. This entry exists because prod shipped without it — Report-Only hid the gap on both environments until OBRS-719 AC 5 made prod's header enforcing, and every one of those thumbnails became a broken-image icon the same day (OBRS-1311). No amount of draining the booking-to-payment journey would have found it: not one of the four surfaces is on that journey.
_obrs888_note: scripts.clarity.ms, c.clarity.ms and c.bing.com are NOT named by any file in this repo, and that is the point: `origins` above lists what a loader's SOURCE names, which is why rule 4 could never have found these. www.clarity.ms/tag/<id> is a bootstrap that fetches scripts.clarity.ms/<ver>/clarity.js; c.clarity.ms/c.gif 302s to c.bing.com/c.gif. Measured on published SIT, OBRS-888. c.bing.com is load-bearing even though no violation report ever names it — CSP re-checks each redirect hop but reports the PRE-redirect URL, so allowing only c.clarity.ms fails under a real enforcing header while producing a report that points at c.clarity.ms. Verified with an enforcing header and a three-arm control, not read off the spec.
_obrs889_note: sitCspOrigins is UNCHANGED by OBRS-889 and that is the finding, not an omission. https://accounts.google.com was already listed — it has been in script-src, connect-src and frame-src since OBRS-719 — yet an enforcing header still dropped https://accounts.google.com/gsi/style, the stylesheet gsi/client injects into our document, because style-src did not name the host. This list is ORIGIN-level, so it is structurally blind to a directive-level gap: both inventory comparisons stay green while the fetch is denied. The rule that does see it is SIDECAR_SUBRESOURCES in check-payment-page-scripts.mjs (script-src implies style-src for this host, whole-token, directional). Measured on published SIT under a real Content-Security-Policy header, 1 violation before / 0 after; the sign-in BUTTON is unaffected either way — it renders inside a cross-origin accounts.google.com iframe that frame-src allows — so the cost of the gap was a collector whose PCI DSS 11.6.1 steady state is zero lines, not a broken login.
_obrs1301_note: sitCspOrigins is UNCHANGED by OBRS-1301, and — as in OBRS-889 — that is the finding rather than an omission. ⛔ READ THIS BEFORE ADDING AN OMISE ORIGIN FOR THE PromptPay QR. https://api.omise.co and https://*.omise.co ARE in the list above, which is exactly the trap _obrs889_note describes: this list is ORIGIN-level, so it cannot say that those entries earn their place in connect-src (tokenisation) and frame-src, and that netlify.toml's img-src names no omise.co origin at all. OBRS-1301 AC-1 required a decision, in writing, between (a) allowlisting the gateway origin ahead of the day the backend forwards Omise's scannable_code and (b) making the code fail loudly instead — its stated reason being that whoever came next would otherwise reverse it silently. The answer is (b), and events overtook the question: OBRS-1351 (2026-08-14) forwarded scannable_code and img-src grew https://api.omise.co PLUS the omise-gateway-production S3 bucket the document URL 302s to, then OBRS-1379 (2026-08-16) served the image from our own GET /api/…/payments/<id>/qr and removed BOTH again. Measured 2026-08-17 with git show on both repos: neither origin/dev nor origin/main carries either origin in img-src, and a0dce431 is an ancestor of origin/main, so the removal is what prod serves. ⛔ Do not re-add one of the pair without the other — CSP re-checks every redirect hop but reports the PRE-redirect URL (OBRS-888), so that state is a QR that renders nowhere and a collector structurally unable to name the host it needs. The half that makes (b) true rather than merely intended lives in the frontend: loadQrImage() passes through only sources with no origin of their own (data:, blob:) and returns '' for anything else, which takes the existing QR_UNAVAILABLE path, so a customer sees a message instead of a blank square under a 15-minute countdown; e2e/tests/obrs-1301-qr-img-src.spec.ts reads img-src out of netlify.toml at run time, re-serves it as an ENFORCING Content-Security-Policy on /payment, and holds a must-catch and a must-NOT-catch arm plus a positive control that proves the header is enforcing at all. AC-2 is retired with AC-1 for the reason that leaves it nothing to do: it was conditional on choosing (a), and there is no origin to add to the four files.
